common_name: Himrod Grape (Cornell-Bred White Seedless Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Himrod, bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York station, is a widely grown early-ripening white seedless table grape; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.

directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Himrod was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and remains one of the most widely planted seedless table grapes for home gardens in cooler climates, producing loose clusters of amber-green, honey-sweet, crisp berries that ripen early in the season. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning to improve berry size. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
University of Minnesota Extension — Grape Growing

common_name: Canadice Grape (Cornell-Bred Red Seedless Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Canadice, bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York station, is a reliably productive red seedless table grape with a mild, sweet, slightly Labrusca-tinged flavor; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.

directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Canadice was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and is a dependable, heavily productive red seedless table grape, bearing compact clusters of small, sweet, mildly Labrusca-flavored berries on a vigorous, cold-hardy vine. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning early in the season to improve berry size and quality. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and insufficient winter chill limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
University of Minnesota Extension — Grape Growing

common_name: Interlaken Grape (Cornell-Bred Early White Seedless Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Interlaken, bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York station, is one of the earliest-ripening white seedless table grapes, a parent of Himrod; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.

directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Interlaken was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station as one of the earliest-ripening seedless table grapes available, producing sweet, crisp, pale green-gold berries in compact clusters well ahead of most other seedless varieties, an advantage for gardeners in shorter-season climates wanting a head start on the grape harvest. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning to improve berry size. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
University of Minnesota Extension — Grape Growing
